solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Distinctive item along with beer bottles

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it up inside a container, so the beer holds the other piece within it

blocks.note: stout is a dark, heavy beer
'along with' means plus, the joining word and

explanation.surface: Someone singles out a striking thing found among the beer bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun beside 'beer', but it is the verb: the beer holds the other piece inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: the thing that stands out from the rest is a standout.

clue.text: Dishonest type of player asking for another card?

blocks.note: a swindler, someone who bends the truth
in pontoon, the British name for blackjack, the call for one more card is 'twist'

explanation.surface: A card cheat is suspected because he keeps asking to be dealt another card.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from 'twist': to twist the truth, and to twist in pontoon, which means taking another card.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are nouns of the agent: one who twists the truth, and one who calls 'twist' at cards.

clue.text: Don’t give up when, in the end, every idea’s worked!

indicators.note: at the end of 'when' sits the single letter wanted
letters that are worked, like dough, are kneaded into a new shape

explanation.surface: A cheer of triumph: persistence paid off and every idea came good.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as encouragement, which is exactly what the answer is; the definition is the opening command.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the imperative 'never say die' is a rallying cry that means keep going.

clue.text: 19th-century designer initially disregarded 18th-century gold lace

indicators.note: what comes initially, the first letter, is disregarded and left out

blocks.note: William Morris, the Victorian textile and wallpaper designer
the designer's name without its first letter M

explanation.surface: A Victorian designer ignored the ornate gold lace of the previous century.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure word, so the wordplay does the work. The two centuries side by side make the clue read like a line of design history.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist historical term: orris named a gold or silver lace fashionable in the 1700s, now found mostly in dictionaries.

clue.text: Mike stops high-pitched vibration

indicators.note: to stop a hole is to plug it, so M plugs a gap inside the other word

blocks.note: Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A microphone cuts out an irritating high-pitched hum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' reads as 'halts', but here it means 'plugs'.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: a tremble is a small shaking movement, which is what a vibration is.

clue.text: Secret report on the core of Scientology

indicators.note: the core of a thing is its centre, here the middle letter of the word

blocks.note: a journalist covers (reports on) a story
middle (sixth) letter of the eleven in SCIENTOLOGY

explanation.surface: A confidential report exposes what lies at the heart of Scientology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret report' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Secret'; 'report on' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: covert operations are secret ones, done under cover.

clue.text: Remnants of slug trail mostly heading up over raised border

definitions.note: plural definition for a singular answer: a spent cartridge is what remains once the slug is fired

indicators.note: most of the word but not all of it, so the last letter goes
in a down entry, a word heading up reads from bottom to top
in a down entry, the piece before 'over' sits above the one after it

blocks.note: TRACK minus its last letter is TRAC, turned upward

explanation.surface: A garden scene: what is left of a slug is its slimy trail heading up over the edge of a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a garden slug; the definition wants a bullet, and the case left behind after firing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic stretch: a slug is a bullet, and once it is fired the cartridge case is what is left behind.

clue.text: Lab specialist perhaps involved in projective tests

indicators.note: the answer is involved, wrapped up, inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A laboratory scientist is running psychological projective tests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lab' seems to be a laboratory, but it is a Labrador dog; 'perhaps' flags that it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a Labrador is one animal a vet specialises in treating.

clue.text: Bird went skyward completely inverted

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a down entry means read upward

blocks.note: went up, past tense of rise

explanation.surface: A bird flew straight up and then flipped right over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Completely' is ALL, and only that piece is inverted.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the rosella is an Australian parrot, so a bird.

clue.text: I bet rats never troubled cockroaches, for instance

indicators.note: troubled water is disturbed, and so are these letters

explanation.surface: Someone wagers that rats never bothered the cockroaches.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pits one pest against another; the definition is by example, marked by 'for instance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: cockroaches are insects with no backbone, one instance of the class.

clue.text: Facts about figures hosting Republican inaugurations

indicators.note: a host has a guest inside the house, so the first word takes the letter in

explanation.surface: Statistics about the ceremonies swearing in Republican presidents.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to presidential inaugurations; the definition just means beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: A general sense: an inauguration is the formal beginning of something, so starts.

clue.text: Farm building with calves regularly occupied by a certain goose

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter
a house occupied by someone has them inside, so A moves in

explanation.surface: A farm barn where the calves are, taken over by a goose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only joins the first two pieces; the whole is then occupied. 'A certain goose' at the end is the definition, not more wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific name: the barnacle goose is a black-and-white Arctic goose, hence 'a certain' one.

clue.text: Using acquired evidence, new operator is beginning to improve

indicators.note: the letters are made new, put into a fresh order
only the beginning, the first letter, of 'improve'

explanation.surface: A new operator, working from evidence gathered, is starting to get better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' sits before 'operator' as a plain adjective, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A philosophical term: Latin for reasoning from experience, the opposite of a priori.

clue.text: Opportunity — with money — to have a meal

blocks.note: a chance, as in 'a lucky break'

explanation.surface: A chance, plus some cash, lets you go out to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'with money' look like an aside, but it is just the second half of the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to break bread with someone is to eat with them.

clue.text: Terrible 11 split open by old Spanish champions

indicators.note: a terrible mess of letters, jumbled out of order
the letters are split open so the other piece can sit inside

blocks.note: the answer to 11 across, used as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A football report: a hopeless eleven torn apart by the old Spanish title-holders.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' reads as a football team but is a cross-reference to the answer at 11 across, scrambled with O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the football club Barcelona have often been Spanish league champions.

clue.text: Fine wine, unopened?

indicators.note: a bottle unopened keeps its top on; here the opening letter is taken off

blocks.note: Tokay is a sweet Hungarian wine
the wine without its first letter T

explanation.surface: A fine wine is still sealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine wine' looks like one phrase; 'Fine' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: saying something is fine is saying it is all right, acceptable.

clue.text: Outstanding leaders from our wonderful head journalist

indicators.note: the leaders of a line of words are their front letters

explanation.surface: Praise for a newspaper's brilliant editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' sounds like praise, but it means unpaid, as a debt is.
explanation.definitionFit: The financial sense: an outstanding bill is one still to be paid.

clue.text: Good job a GPS might show this!

explanation.surface: Praise for a satnav's directions.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is literal: a GPS shows the route you should take, and the same three words are a cheer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the exclamation 'way to go!' means well done, and literally the route a GPS displays.

clue.text: Property made of concrete close to Boise, Idaho?

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter

blocks.note: Idaho is a US state; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: A building made of concrete near Boise, the capital of Idaho.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concrete' looks like building material but means actual; 'Idaho?' stands in by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainly American term: land and buildings as property are real estate.

clue.text: Passages by artist written up for magazine

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means set down from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Pieces by an artist are written up for a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magazine' is not a periodical but a store for weapons and ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: The military sense: a magazine is a store of arms and ammunition, which is what an arsenal is.

clue.text: Label containing information about hard wood

indicators.note: about can mean around, so the label goes around the letter

blocks.note: a tag giving price or details

explanation.surface: A tag giving details about some hardwood timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard wood' reads as a timber type; split it, and 'hard' is the letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a thicket is a dense patch of shrubs and small trees, a small wood.

clue.text: Pile of combustible material noticed around range

indicators.note: turned around to face the other way, so read backwards

blocks.note: a heap of wood for burning, especially a funeral one

explanation.surface: Someone spots a heap of firewood near the cooking stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests a kitchen stove; it is a line of mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the Pyrenees are the mountain range dividing France from Spain.

clue.text: Line taken by nearly all sea fish

indicators.note: the line is taken in by the other word, held inside it
nearly all of the word, just short of its last letter

blocks.note: MARINE (of the sea) without its last letter

explanation.surface: An angler's line is grabbed by almost every fish in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea' here is the adjective MARINE, cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the marlin is a large ocean game fish.

clue.text: Word from Larousse provided recurring theme

blocks.note: French for word; Larousse is a French dictionary

explanation.surface: A French dictionary supplies a word that keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: Larousse signals French, so the word is the French one.
explanation.definitionFit: An arts term: in music, literature or design, a motif is an element that keeps recurring.

clue.text: Rowdy bloke not prepared for group of influential guys

indicators.note: food that is prepared is chopped and rearranged; so are these letters

explanation.surface: A loud man isn't ready for the company of powerful men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowdy' looks like an anagram indicator, but it is fodder; 'prepared' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the informal web of powerful men who went to the same schools.

clue.text: Drop of creamy mixture

blocks.note: a fall, as in prices or a road
a sauce you scoop with crisps or raw vegetables

explanation.surface: Just a drop of some creamy mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop of' reads as 'a little of', but 'of' only joins two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Two noun senses: a small fall or decline, and a thick sauce for dipping food into.

clue.text: Big commotion as a large, friendly bear comes back

indicators.note: what comes back returns the way it went, so everything before it reads backwards

explanation.surface: A great fuss erupts when a big, friendly bear returns.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run of pieces reverses, not just the bear, so A ends up last.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal noun synonym: hoopla is noisy fuss and excitement, a big commotion.

clue.text: Liberal English newspaper is ultimately just tedious for Labour supporters, say

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the end letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A left-leaning English paper is simply boring to Labour voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' tempts as the definition, but it is just a letter. Labour is the British left-wing party, and 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Labour is Britain's main left-wing party, so its supporters are one kind of leftist.
